title: Why Did Millions of People Quit Their Jobs?

segments.label: scene 1 (title)
segments.text: In late 2021, something historic happened across the labor market. Millions of workers handed in their notices, walking away from their jobs at a record pace.

segments.label: scene 2 (counter)
segments.text: By November 2021, the monthly quit rate hit 3.0%. That was the highest level ever recorded by the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

segments.label: scene 3 (waffle)
segments.text: To put that in perspective, 3.0% of the entire voluntary workforce handed in their notice in just a single month.

segments.label: scene 4 (line)
segments.text: Just eighteen months earlier, in April 2020, fear had frozen the market. The quit rate plummeted to a record low of 1.5%.

segments.label: scene 5 (statement)
segments.text: As lockdowns lifted, that fear turned into unprecedented mobility. Commentators quickly gave this massive wave a name: The Great Resignation.

segments.label: scene 6 (heatmap)
segments.text: Compared to the pre-pandemic rate of 2.3% in January 2020, workers were jumping ship at unheard-of speeds.

segments.label: scene 7 (gauge)
segments.text: Why did so many people quit all at once? The answer lies in a complete shift in leverage and worker priorities.

segments.label: scene 8 (statement)
segments.text: To understand the historic wave of resignations, we must first look at how turnover and hiring behaved during a typical economic expansion.

segments.label: scene 9 (counter)
segments.text: In January 2015, the voluntary monthly quit rate sat at just 2.0%.

segments.label: scene 10 (line)
segments.text: Meanwhile, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, the overall US unemployment rate stood at 5.7%.

segments.label: scene 11 (multiline)
segments.text: As the economic expansion deepened, falling joblessness began boosting confidence across the workforce.

segments.label: scene 12 (compare)
segments.text: By February 2019, an earlier spike pushed the quit rate to 2.4%, marking a 9% increase in the year before it.

segments.label: scene 13 (counter)
segments.text: The labor market continued tightening right up to the pandemic, bringing unemployment down to 3.6% in January 2020.

segments.label: scene 14 (kpi)
segments.text: Looking across the entire period from January 2020 to October 2026, unemployment ultimately saw a change of +14%.

segments.label: scene 15 (counter)
segments.text: Then came the spring of 2020. Lockdowns shut down entire industries, sending economic shockwaves everywhere. By April 2020, US unemployment skyrocketed to a peak of 14.8%.

segments.label: scene 16 (statement)
segments.text: Workers prioritized stability over new opportunities. Quitting ground to a halt as health risks and economic uncertainty took hold.

segments.label: scene 17 (line)
segments.text: Yet beneath the immediate chaos, wage dynamics were quietly shifting. In January 2020, average hourly pay sat at $23.91.

segments.label: scene 18 (compare)
segments.text: As federal aid arrived and businesses reopened, hiring roared back. From that record peak down to October 2026, the unemployment rate collapsed by -72%.

segments.label: scene 19 (line)
segments.text: Worker demand quickly outpaced supply. By April 2023, unemployment dropped to a record low of 3.4%.

segments.label: scene 20 (statement)
segments.text: Employers suddenly faced severe labor shortages, forcing companies to compete aggressively for talent.

segments.label: scene 21 (kpi)
segments.text: By October 2026, average hourly pay reached $32.75, up +37% from January 2020. That sudden surge in leverage set off a historic chain reaction.

segments.label: scene 22 (statement)
segments.text: As businesses reopened after lockdowns, desperation to hire sparked intense wage competition across nearly every industry. Employers suddenly fought fiercely for available workers.

segments.label: scene 23 (counter)
segments.text: Pay had already been climbing before the crisis. Back in January 2015, average hourly pay for non-managers sat at $20.80.

segments.label: scene 24 (line)
segments.text: That baseline grew rapidly over the following decade. From January 2015 to October 2026, average hourly pay surged by +57%.

segments.label: scene 25 (statement)
segments.text: Job switchers gained unprecedented leverage over stayers. Quitting handed workers immediate bargaining power, making job hopping the fastest shortcut to higher pay.

segments.label: scene 26 (compare)
segments.text: Even as economic conditions normalized, pay kept grinding higher. Between January 2025 and October 2026, average hourly pay increased another +6%.

segments.label: scene 27 (line)
segments.text: Meanwhile, joblessness remained low by historical standards. By October 2026, the US unemployment rate sat at 4.1%.

segments.label: scene 28 (heatmap)
segments.text: As extreme labor shortages finally eased, voluntary turnover cooled off. From its historic high in November 2021 to September 2026, the quit rate fell -30%.

segments.label: scene 29 (statement)
segments.text: As the extreme churn of previous years faded, a far more balanced labor market gradually took shape across the country.

segments.label: scene 30 (counter)
segments.text: By September 2026, the voluntary monthly quit rate had settled down to 2.1%.

segments.label: scene 31 (line)
segments.text: Even with that broader cooling, turnover edged back up over the final stretch. From September 2025 to September 2026, the quit rate increased +10.5%.

segments.label: scene 32 (gauge)
segments.text: That gentle uptick showed that workers still felt confident enough to pursue better career opportunities.

segments.label: scene 33 (line)
segments.text: Unemployment also maintained a healthy baseline. Between November 2025 and October 2026, the US unemployment rate dropped -8.9%.

segments.label: scene 34 (bars)
segments.text: Looking across the longer horizon from January 2015 to October 2026, overall unemployment saw a net change of -28%.

segments.label: scene 35 (counter)
segments.text: At the same time, pay growth normalized into a steady pattern, with average hourly pay reaching $32.75 by October 2026.

segments.label: scene 36 (statement)
segments.text: The wave of resignations did not just disrupt workplaces for a few crazy years; it fundamentally rewrote the rules of employment.

segments.label: scene 37 (line)
segments.text: Even as hiring normalized, mobility stayed resilient. From January 2025 to September 2026, the quit rate climbed another +5%.

segments.label: scene 38 (multiline)
segments.text: Workers secured permanent baseline pay gains and lasting expectations for flexibility. Higher compensation is now baked into the broader labor market.

segments.label: scene 39 (bars)
segments.text: The dynamic between employer power and employee choice has permanently shifted, giving workers far more leverage than previous generations enjoyed.

segments.label: scene 40 (gauge)
segments.text: Ultimately, mass quitting peaked at 3.0% in November 2021 — not as a temporary panic, but as the opening chapter of a brand new labor landscape where the entire economy adapts.
